articles.title: Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
articles.snippet: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have announced a "return hub" for failed asylum seekers.
articles.full_text:
Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
- Published
Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.
The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.
Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.
The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024.
Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".
The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.
In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.
In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".
Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.
Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".
He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".
Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.
The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.
"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".
With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.
Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries.
Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.
"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."
The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.
The agency added that unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, which the Dutch government has confirmed will not take place.
According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.
In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

articles.title: Five EU countries announce plan to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera

articles.full_text:
Five EU countries announce plan to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda
In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan.
Five European countries have announced a plan to send rejected asylum seekers to a processing centre in Rwanda as early as next year, drawing condemnation from rights groups who said it would leave vulnerable people at risk of abuse.
The planned scheme, which is still being negotiated with Rwanda, would send people to a centre where the migrants could choose to return home, settle or go somewhere else where they had a right to stay, Kigali said on Monday.

Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands said that the plan aimed to deter more people from migrating to Europe. The European Union has worked for years to tighten migration rules, reduce the number of asylum seekers arriving and increase deportations of migrants who are not entitled to stay.
“I think this will be a game changer, making us able to confront the massive challenges with illegal migration,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said. “We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders and we will remove the incentives for illegal migration.”
Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, said his country would give a “second chance” to people who have no right to stay in Europe.
He added that arrivals would be able “to voluntarily return to the countries of origin, integrate into Rwandan society or relocate to another destination where they have the legal right to reside, according to their preference”.
When asked how Kigali would ensure refugees’ human rights, Biruta said, “There will be an independent monitoring mechanism” and that it would cooperate with the United Nations’ refugee agency.
Human rights groups criticised the plans, saying that EU countries could not guarantee their rights would be respected there.
In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan — echoing criticisms of a different migration settlement plan between Britain and Rwanda in the early 2020s.
The plan “signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” read the statement from the International Rescue Committee, the Dutch Council for Refugees and other groups.
A Human Rights Watch researcher said the deal “would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad”.
Germany’s interior minister said the European plan was not comparable to a scrapped 2022 deal with the United Kingdom because only those whose asylum claims are rejected will be sent to Rwanda.
The UK’s Supreme Court ruled that the 2022 deal was unlawful because Rwanda was not considered a safe third country to which migrants could be sent.

articles.title: Yemeni forces retreat to defend port city from Houthis
articles.snippet: Saudi-backed forces say they are moving troops from the Bab al-Mandab Strait to protect the interim capital, Aden.
articles.full_text:
Yemeni forces retreat to defend port city from Houthis
- Published
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they are redeploying troops to defend the country's interim capital, Aden, following weeks of intensified fighting with the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
The Southern Armed Forces said it was withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea, to reinforce positions around Aden and neighbouring areas.
Houthi-run media say the movement has taken control of the evacuated territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.
The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the key shipping route which the Houthis seized in a surprise offensive in September.
Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis. The Iran-backed fighters said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.
But the Saudi-backed Southern Armed Forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".
It said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area" with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".
"This step is driven by the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and neighbouring governorates, reinforcing the front lines and addressing existing threats."
The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured territory overlooking it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.
A UN Human Rights spokesperson, Ravina Shamdasani, urged all parties to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.
She noted that since the escalation of fighting in August, more than 60% of documented civilian casualties were women and children.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Aden in recent weeks, including an assault on 15 October that targeted the presidential palace, killing five and injuring 16.
Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure.
The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.
Yemeni military says it has 'secured' Red Sea waterway
- Published6 October

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from its capital, Sanaa.
The conflict escalated in 2015 after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

articles.title: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
articles.snippet: A number of tech figures want the board of the AI chip giant to give Jensen Huang his job back.
articles.full_text:
Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executive called for him to be reinstated.
Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.
It created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms, which is a key part of the AI rollout, but the BBC has been told Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Huang.
Meanwhile the Trump administration on Monday said it will further restrict China's âaccess to AI chips from companies like Nvidia.
Fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have backed a campaign to get Nvidia's board to "Bring Jensen Back".
The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.
"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.
The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models.
The move came ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jingping.
The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted to China.
The president's comments on Huang came after the "Stand with Jensen" campaign group, which claims to be made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, demanded the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.
However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times, external, though the publication reported Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.
A person familiar with the thinking of Nvidia's board told the BBC its directors are not interested in bringing Huang back to lead the company.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal broke out, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".
Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
'China plays games with us, so we play games with China'
On Monday, Trump said he did not know whether the women Huang had an affair with was a spy for China.
"They say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't, I don't know that." he said.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
'A handshake with Jensen'
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X., external
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."
But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.
Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

articles.title: Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war
articles.snippet: Russia said Ukraine had launched over 2,000 drones over the course of a day, while Kyiv came under a record 17 air raid alerts.
articles.full_text:
Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war
- Published
Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.
The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.
Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people.
The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war.
The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.
The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.
Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate has responded to a BBC request for comment.
Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.
Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.
Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.
Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect.
Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and give up efforts to become a Nato member.
The Kremlin has now also started to talk again about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia.
The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.
A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US.
But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input.
"We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov.
EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

articles.title: Forensic expert says his analysis of autopsy photos suggest Epstein was killed
articles.snippet: Professor Michael Freeman tells BBC Newsnight that he believes the convicted sex offender's injuries are consistent with a homicide.
articles.full_text:
Forensic expert says his analysis of autopsy photos suggest Epstein was killed
- Published
This article contains distressing details and references to suicide
A forensic expert has said he believes that convicted sex offender Jeffery Epstein's death in prison was the result of a homicide, not suicide.
Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor Michael Freeman said that after reviewing the New York City medical examiner's file he believes Epstein was strangled, most likely from behind.
The medical examiner who carried out the autopsy concluded in 2019 that Epstein's injuries were consistent with suicide and there was no evidence of the defensive wounds expected if his death had been a homicide.
Epstein was found dead in prison on 10 August 2019 in New York as he awaited trial on sex trafficking charges.
Dr Barbara Sampson, chief medical examiner at the time of Epstein's autopsy, who ruled that Epstein's death was a suicide, has previously said: "I stand firmly behind our determination of the cause and manner of death for Mr. Epstein." The BBC has approached Sampson for further comment.
Freeman has served as a cause-of-death expert to attorneys-general in the US for death in police custody cases, including George Floyd in Minnesota.
He published his research and the New York City medical examiner's files after presenting his findings in London on Monday evening.
Freeman, who did not see the body, based his conclusions on the files and photographs from the examiner's report provided to him by Epstein's brother, Mark Epstein, who has always maintained that his brother was murdered.
Freeman said his analysis is independent and that he was not paid by Mark Epstein. His research has not been peer reviewed.
He told the BBC that he believed there are signs indicating an assault on Epstein, including a deep haemorrhage to his left shoulder and injuries that appear to be consistent to being struck in the face.
Freeman said he believed the evidence was most consistent with strangulation using a ligature and then that same ligature was probably used to suspend the body from the bunk bed.
He said there appeared to be fingernail marks above the ligature mark on Epstein's neck, which "would be consistent with strangulation, particularly from behind. And the attempt by the victim to try to remove the ligature from the neck".
He said "the injuries and the way the body was found don't match up. There's only one remaining explanation then, and that is that the death was as a result of a homicide."
The medical examiner who performed the autopsy at the time told the Department of Justice (DoJ) Office of the Inspector General , externalthat Epstein's injuries were more consistent with, and indicative of, a suicide by hanging rather than homicide by strangulation, adding there was no evidence of defensive wounds consistent with what is seen in victims of strangulation.
Freeman said he would have expected in an investigation of a death by hanging in custody for there to be a photograph before the body was taken down.
According to a DoJ investigation into Epstein's time in prison, the guard who found Epstein immediately called for a second colleague to help, lowered Epstein's body to the floor and began attempts to resuscitate him.
Epstein's death came a month after he was briefly placed on suicide watch, the DoJ report said.
When asked who might have killed Epstein if his interpretation of the evidence was correct, Freeman said he had "no idea".
"That is not something I have an opinion about. That isn't any part of any investigation that I've done," he said.
Challenged on whether his views veered into conspiracy theory, Freeman said: "I have the luxury of being able to say, don't take my word for it, let everybody look at it."
"If you think I'm still a conspiracy theorist because I'm looking at something that looks like a strangulation and say, I think it is a strangulation and I don't think it could be a hanging, show me where I got it wrong."
"I'm wide open to that. I'm an academic. I'm quite happy to hear people's theories on things that are informed," he said.
Epstein was convicted in 2008 of soliciting prostitution from a minor, for which he was registered as a sex offender. He escaped a heavy jail sentence as a result of a plea deal.
Eleven years later, Epstein was charged with running a network of underage girls for sex. He was awaiting trial in 2019 when he was found dead at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York City.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial next year for deaths of her three children
articles.snippet: The 36-year-old's first trial this year fell apart when a 12-person jury failed to reach a verdict.
articles.full_text:
Lindsay Clancy to face retrial next year for deaths of her three children
- Published
Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.
Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children, will face a retrial next year, a judge has said, after a jury deadlocked last time in a case that gripped the nation.
The judge set a trial date for 29 March 2027, though the district attorney did not explicitly say what charges Clancy would face.
Prosecutors said they wanted a jury trial, and the defence said they took that to mean Clancy, 36, would again face first-degree murder charges.
Five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan were strangled at the family home on 24 January 2023. The defence argues she had severe postpartum psychosis.
"I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA [district attorney] that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments, so we will pick a trial date," defence lawyer Kevin Reddington said at Monday's hearing.
Prosecutors wanted a May trial date, but Judge William Sullivan decided on March instead. The judge is due to retire in June.
Clancy was charged in the first trial with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.
The district attorney has not yet officially said he will proceed with first-degree-murder charges. The BBC has contacted the district attorney's office for comment.
The prosecution could choose to bring lesser charges against Clancy, such as second-degree-murder, which applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without planning.
A week ago, Judge Sullivan rejected a defence attempt to throw out the case on the grounds of double jeopardy.
Double jeopardy is a legal principle that protects someone from being prosecuted more than once for the same crime after an acquittal or conviction.
The judge's decision cleared the way for a second trial. It was Judge Sullivan who declared the mistrial on 4 September because of the hung jury.
Afterwards, some of the 12 jurors said in media interviews that they had been ready to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, but that one juror had held out.
It was not disputed at Clancy's first trial that she strangled the children with exercise bands in the basement of the family home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury.
She had asked her now-ex husband, Patrick Clancy, to leave the house to pick up takeout food and children's medicine shortly before the children were attacked.
The defence team wanted her found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.
The case sparked a debate over how postpartum mental illness is treated in the US.
Clancy is currently in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts.

articles.title: Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 17 dead
articles.snippet: The shootings in KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng highlight South Africa's struggle to curb violent crime.
articles.full_text:
Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 17 dead
- Published
South African police are investigating the murders of 17 people in two separate shootings on Sunday night.
Eight men were fatally shot in a minibus in KwaZulu-Natal province. Police declared them dead when they arrived at the scene. Hours later, nine people were found shot dead inside a shack in western Pretoria.
Police say the two incidents are unrelated. The motive for the shootings has not yet been established.
South Africa is struggling to contain violent crime, including gang-related killings. The country has one of the world's highest murder rates.
Police say they responded to reports of a shooting â outside Pietermaritzburg town in KwaZulu-Natal and found a white seven-seater vehicle riddled with bullet holes.
Inside were eight men with multiple gunshot wounds.
"It has not been established how the incident happened, and police are collecting pieces of evidence to determine the possible motive of the killings and the identity of the suspects," police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said.
The police have launched a manhunt for the suspects.
In a separate shooting in the Jeffsville informal settlement in Atteridgeville, west of Pretoria, police found the bodies of six men and three women.
They are believed to have been killed inside a four-room shack between 22:00 and 23:00 on Sunday. The bodies were scattered across the rooms, with several spent cartridges discovered outside the shack.
Community members initially mistook the gunshots for thunder and lightning.
"The provincial commissioner of police in Gauteng [province, which includes Pretoria] has mobilized the necessary resources, including the crime intelligence and the deputy provincial commissioner tracking team to search for the suspect," police spokesperson Brigadier Brenda Muridili said.
It's not the first mass shooting in the area. In January, five men were shot dead outside a local shop in broad daylight.
Illegal firearms are widespread in South Africa, where gun violence remains a persistent problem, increasingly involving mass shootings.
In September, 28 people were killed in two separate cases.
Eighteen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar near Johannesburg and opened fire on 25 September. Fourteen others were injured.
In a separate shooting the following day, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town. A further 11 were injured.
Much of the violence has been linked to turf wars between gangs involved in drug trafficking and illegal mining.
In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa described organised crime as "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development".
Earlier this year, the military was deployed alongside police to five provinces with the highest murder rates, including Gauteng, in an effort to tackle armed violence.
According to the latest police statistics, 5,427 people were murdered nationwide between April and June 2026, an average of about 60 killings a day. This was a 6% decline compared with the same period a year earlier.
Additional reporting by Christian Parkinson in Johannesburg

articles.full_text:
Inside Story
What will Europe do next in Ukraine?
There is division within the European Union over diplomatic strategy for efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukrainian cities as Kyiv’s forces continue to carry out long-range strikes.
But diplomatic pressure is ramping up, too, with the European Union wanting a say in United States-brokered talks aimed at ending Russia and Ukraine’s four-and-a-half-year war.
So, what role should Europe play?

articles.title: Nationwide ground stop could cost US airlines hundreds of millions
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Airline executives support modernising FAA systems as US Transportation Secretary Duffy seeks $50bn from Congress.
articles.full_text:
Nationwide ground stop could cost US airlines hundreds of millions
Airline executives support modernising FAA systems as US Transportation Secretary Duffy seeks $50bn from Congress for FAA overhaul.
Following the nationwide ground stop last week, United States airlines could face a financial hit of hundreds of millions of dollars even as airline executives press for increased investment in ageing air traffic control infrastructure.
The four largest US airlines – American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines – could face a combined hit of $345m to pretax earnings, according to brokerage firm Bernstein.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Trump denies responsibility for FAA nationwide ground stop
- list 2 of 3What forced the US to ground all planes? A router switch, we now know
- list 3 of 3After a nationwide ground stop, US faces aviation infrastructure questions
The effects of Friday’s ground stop continued to ripple through airline schedules on Monday, with more than 18,500 flights within, into or out of the US cancelled since the disruption began, according to FlightAware data.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC on Monday that the wider impact of the disruption could run into the “billions of dollars”. No official estimate of the total economic cost has been released yet.
Flights were grounded across the country for more than four hours on Friday, and the disruption continued to affect airline schedules over the weekend.
Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian also said the financial impact could run into the “billions”, telling Fortune on Monday that the disruption underscored the need for greater investment in the country’s air traffic control infrastructure.
Bastian pointed to the vast sums investors are putting into artificial intelligence and data centres, adding that the US should also be investing in its aviation system.
“We can’t even get $50bn to fix our skies,” he said.
United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby agreed that the disruption should be a “call to action”, saying the air traffic control system needed greater investment in modern technology to improve its reliability.
Transportation Secretary Duffy has asked US Congress for $50bn for air traffic control and airport infrastructure upgrades, an addition to the $12.5bn lawmakers approved for air traffic control modernisation last year.
The existing system relies on outdated equipment and needs a comprehensive overhaul, he said.
But Democrats have questioned the request, saying only about $1bn of the $12.5bn already approved has been spent so far.
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump called on Congress to approve the funding, arguing that the upgrades should be carried out all at once rather than in stages.
“We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The funding debate is moving into a narrow window for congressional action. The House and Senate are scheduled to convene once more before the end of the year.
Speaker Mike Johnson has said lawmakers will take up the administration’s funding request during the current Congress’s lame-duck session, but Democrats have demanded more information on how the money will be spent.
The precise cause of Friday’s failure remains under investigation. Duffy has said the problem began at a remote Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) site in Arkansas where workers from defence contractor L3Harris were replacing ageing copper wiring with fibre-optic cables.
The Government Accountability Office, the congressional watchdog, raised concerns about the FAA’s management of its modernisation programme in a September report. It found that the agency had not developed an integrated schedule for the first phase of upgrades, and warned that poor planning increased the risk of disrupting air traffic control operations.

Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of attempted ‘coup’
Political rivals call for investigation regarding media reports that Netanyahu’s office tried to frame Arab party members ahead of the elections.
Israeli opposition leaders have denounced an “attempted coup” by outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The accusations on Monday came in response to media reports that Netanyahu’s office tried to falsely incriminate members of an Arab-led party before last month’s election, in which the premier’s Likud party was voted out of office.
Recommended Stories

- list 3 of 4Who is Ahmad Tibi, the Arab MP elected deputy speaker of Israel’s Knesset?
- list 4 of 4Is Israel’s Eisenkot bloc less right wing than Netanyahu?
“As more and more details come to light, it becomes clear: This wasn’t an attempt to disrupt the elections. It was an attempted coup,” opposition leader Yair Lapid said on social media.
Israel’s Channel 12 reported on Sunday that on the eve of the election, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, called police with a complaint about members of the Ra’am party.
Norden reportedly pointed officers to a purported intelligence source – a former employee of Netanyahu’s office – who provided information that led to the arrest of three Ra’am members. They were later released after police determined the allegations were unfounded.
Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported on Sunday that the head of the Shin Bet domestic security service tried to wiretap leaders of the Arab-led Joint List, but the attorney general refused due to a lack of evidence.
Israeli police said in response that they will “review the decision-making and information-transmission process”. Likud has issued a statement denying the reports.
Following the vote, Netanyahu accused Arab parties of electoral fraud after they gained a record 19 seats in the Knesset.
‘Dark regime’
Yousef Jabareen, the leader of Joint List also decried “an attempted coup by Netanyahu,” and labelled the allegations regarding Shin Bet as “conduct characteristic of dark regimes”.
Ra’am deputy and former police chief Yoav Segalovitz called for an urgent investigation.
“Netanyahu cried out that his election was being stolen, while he himself tried to steal the country and is still trying to do so now,” he wrote on social media.
Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, wrote that departing prime minister was “a concrete, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy”.
Neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor Eisenkot’s opposition grouping secured the 61 seats required to form a government. However, Joint List and Raam have indicated they support Eisenkot to lead a coalition.

Saudi Arabia dismisses commander of coalition forces fighting Houthis
Move comes as government forces withdraw from Red Sea coast to halt Houthi approach to interim capital Aden.
Saudi Arabia has replaced the commander overseeing its coalition forces as they battle the Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen.
King Salman issued a decree on Monday assigning General Fayyad al-Ruwaili to the command, according to Saudi state media. The removal of Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad al-Salman came as coalition forces were forced to abandon their recent push to recapture regions along the Red Sea coast in order to reinforce the Yemeni government’s interim capital, Aden.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Houthis edge closer to Aden as Yemeni forces pull out of Bab al-Mandeb
- list 2 of 4Fighting intensifies in Yemen as Houthis deny targeting Mecca
- list 3 of 4Saudi-led coalition intercepts suspected Houthi missiles and drones
- list 4 of 4Siege fuels disease fears in Yemen’s Taiz
Al-Salman was appointed as a military adviser to the Saudi defence minister a day after coalition forces were forced to withdraw.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government said on Sunday that coalition forces were withdrawing from areas near the key Bab al-Mandeb strait – via which Saudi oil exports have been flowing while the United States-Iran war stifles traffic through the Strait of Hormuz – to focus on defending Aden.
The retreat marked a major setback for the Saudi-backed campaign against the Houthis, who have been firing ballistic missiles at Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil facilities since Yemen’s civil war restarted in July.
A Houthi offensive in September saw the government lose control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the key port city of Mocha. Later Houthi advances also saw Taiz completely besieged by the Houthis.
Government forces – backed by the Saudi-led coalition – quickly retook key positions near Bab al-Mandeb after the Houthi advance on the strait and the Red Sea coast this summer, but have been unable to retake Mocha.
They have said they killed or wounded 173 Houthi fighters as part of Operation Dawn of Yemen and engaged the Houthis in Marib, Lahij and in al-Jawf.
However, they are now retreating from theterritory they held near the Bab al-Mandeb strait and preparing to fortify defences around Aden, after the Houthis advanced to an area 60 kilometres (37 miles) north of the city.
Yemeni Armed Forces spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili defended the retreat, saying it was part of a wider tactical manoeuvre.
“[The redeployment] is an extension of the heroic positions of the popular resistance and the southern forces in protecting the temporary capital Aden,” he said on X.
As the fighting continues, civilians remain exposed. Houthi-affiliated media reported coalition air strikes on the capital Sanaa, which the Iran-backed group took in 2014, and said one person was killed in an attack on a school in Taiz.
Authorities in the besieged city of Taiz have called for humanitarian corridors to allow civilians to evacuate, as medical officials warned hospitals could be forced to end operations within two days due to a lack of fuel and oxygen.
Earlier on Monday, Saudi Arabia said it had shot down two Houthi drones targeting the Mecca and Riyadh regions.

At Wells Fargo, for example, more than 800 customers reported issues, including problems with logins, account balances and fund transfers. At Chase, nearly 5,000 customers reported issues, 50 percent of which involved account balances and transactions.

articles.title: US Army takes ‘urgent’ action to build concrete bunkers across the Middle East
articles.snippet: The Army acknowledged in a notice Friday that U.S. soldiers in the Middle East are "currently at risk" using personnel shelters made of converted shipping containers.
articles.full_text:
Fearing for the safety of American troops, the U.S. Army will build concrete bunkers across the Middle East.
The Army wants 17 bunkers capable of remaining intact through indirect fire attacks, such as from missiles and drones. Ten bunkers are planned for Israel, five in Saudi Arabia and two in Lebanon, according to an Army notice posted Friday.
The bunkers are meant to replace current personnel shelters made of converted shipping containers, the notice says.
“Due to elevated regional force protection conditions, there is an urgent, high-priority requirement to replace nonstandard personnel protection shelters (e.g., converted shipping containers) and provide standardized, precast, reinforced concrete Indirect Fire bunkers,” states the Army’s Sources Sought notice. The deadline for companies to respond to the notice is Nov. 25.
“The objective is to safeguard U.S. and coalition service members operating in potentially hostile environments across multiple countries in [U.S. Central Command] Area of Responsibility,” the notice continues.
The project comes after Iranian missiles and drones devastated multiple American bases in the Persian Gulf and killed at least 23 personnel. This includes a March 2026 strike on an Army command post in Kuwait that killed six service members. Subsequent reports allege that the site was poorly protected against aerial bombardment.
The Army did not specify the exact locations of the new bunkers.
“Specific base installation names and coordinates” will be released only to eligible contractors once the actual solicitation is released,” the Army said.
Still, the notice refers to the bunkers being emplaced at five “primary installation” sites: one in Israel and two each in Saudi Arabia and Lebanon.
The bunkers appear to be standardized designs meant for quick construction, rather than elaborate fortifications. Each bunker will consist of three sections of reinforced concrete with steel entrance doors and concrete Alaska barriers shielding the entrances. Sandbags will provide additional protection to the exterior walls, and more layers of sandbags will add at least 18 inches of cover to the roof.
The Army intends to move fast. The notice emphasizes that the project must be completed within 45 days after the task order.
“Due to extreme operational urgency (soldiers currently at risk using non-standard containerized shelters), the subsequent solicitation is anticipated to have an expedited 3-day quote turnaround window,” the notice states.
To make this happen, the Army is looking for “qualified, capable, and licensed construction and engineering firms with immediate cross-border and local mobilization capabilities in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the State of Israel, and the Republic of Lebanon.”
Contractors must specify whether they are bidding to operate in all three nations or only specific countries.

articles.title: Europe hunts for Palantir alternatives as militaries seek to limit US dependence
articles.snippet: Europe's defense ministries are looking to limit dependency on American technology and major software company Palantir Technologies.
articles.full_text:
As Europe’s defense ministries look to limit dependency on American technology and major software company Palantir Technologies for critical military functions, a growing number of firms within the region are competing for their business.
Last week, Germany’s Helsing unveiled military intelligence software called Clarity. It is part of a broader market for AI-powered systems designed to accelerate military decision-making by helping sift through vast quantities of data to identify threats and recommend action, including targeting and attacks.
But Europe currently lacks an exact equivalent that matches Palantir’s scale, deployment footprint and operational experience, some government and military officials say.
That gives European militaries a dilemma: pursue homegrown systems that promise greater autonomy but may be less mature, or rely on a proven platform despite concerns about long-term strategic dependence.
The Trump administration has pushed Europe to take on much greater responsibility for its own security as Washington scales back its military presence in the region, and has placed pressure on the transatlantic NATO alliance.
European officials face similar trade-offs between autonomy and capability across a range of military capabilities, including in the area of satellite communications, which is dominated by Elon Musk’s US company SpaceX.
Ukraine last week reported further significant disruptions of its access to SpaceX, affecting the entire front line and Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
France, a vocal advocate for European autonomy, is developing a sovereign AI-enabled military platform called Arcadia. Alexandre Lahousse, the deputy head of France’s defense procurement agency, told Reuters it would include multiple suppliers. The agency plans to award at least some contracts by year’s end and to have an operational version available for field deployment by mid-2027, he said.
Germany, which is also aiming to deploy an AI-based military data integration platform from next year, is weighing domestic and other European options.
It has narrowed down a shortlist to a handful of solutions, which does not include Palantir, a person familiar with the matter said. The person said the solutions under consideration would not match Palantir’s capabilities but would be good enough, ensure national data sovereignty and should be able to achieve about 80% of what is needed within a year.
The Netherlands currently uses some Palantir software but says it wants a European alternative within two years. The Dutch military is meeting potential suppliers and will likely require a combination of Dutch and other European providers, Dutch arms procurement minister Derk Boswijk told Reuters.
“We have a lot of knowledge in Europe when it comes to AI and decision-making. But it’s very fragmented, and that is the problem,” Boswijk said.
Palantir’s Maven Smart System has been widely used by Ukraine in its fight against Russia while the Pentagon has adopted it as its core military software and has used it in its war with Iran this year.
“I’ve yet to find anything that can pull together as much of a diverse set of data and allow us the ability to make sense of that data as flexibly,” NATO’s top commander, US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, told Reuters this summer.
NATO’s military headquarters adopted Palantir’s Maven Smart System last year and said in June that it was ready for routine alliance-wide operational use.
Militaries are wrestling with many questions, including around data security, who trains the AI systems, and ensuring different platforms work seamlessly together, said Lieutenant General Christian Freuding, Germany’s army chief, at a conference in Berlin on Friday.
“There’s the issue of interoperability when we fight in alliances — and we always fight in alliances.”
NATO officials have previously warned of an increased threat from Russia, which they say could potentially mount a large-scale assault on allied territory as early as 2029. Moscow denies aggressive intentions.
Helsing said it could supply an initial version of its Clarity software within a matter of months to the German military’s Lithuania brigade, widely viewed as the Bundeswehr unit most likely to see frontline combat in the event of a conflict with Russia.
Other European makers of military software include Denmark’s Systematic, whose SitaWare product is used by the Bundeswehr and parts of NATO, as well as traditional defense companies like France’s Thales and Safran, plus startups such as Paris-based Comand AI.
For its part, Palantir has sought to reassure Europeans that its military AI system used by NATO has no “kill switch.” Palantir’s international chief Louis Mosley told Reuters there remains demand in Europe for its products including in the UK, where the defense ministry last year signed a three-year enterprise agreement with the US company.
Mosley added he still hopes to persuade Germany to adopt Palantir’s software with the pitch that it has battlefield-tested capability that works today.

articles.title: China has ‘normalized’ naval presence near Japan since political spat of 2025
articles.snippet: Given its scale, the massive Chinese flotilla that included coast guard vessels alongside navy warships may have had Taiwan’s maritime neighbor Japan in its sights, military experts say.
articles.full_text:
NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan — In early November, Taiwan’s National Security Council secretary-general tracked more than 100 Chinese military-linked vessels near his island.
But given its scale, the massive flotilla that included coast guard vessels alongside navy warships may have had Taiwan’s maritime neighbor Japan in its sights, military experts say.
They say China has sent an outsized number of its far-seas naval deployments to near Japan’s southernmost islands and nearby waters since a political dispute that erupted in November 2025 over a remark by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Takaichi told a Japanese House of Representatives committee session that month that a Chinese naval blockade or armed conflict involving Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for her own country not far away. China claims self-ruled Taiwan as its own and has not ruled out the use of force to take it.
“There is a direct link between Takaichi’s statement and the quality and quantity of deployments,” said Stephen Nagy, a visiting fellow with the Japan Institute for International Affairs think tank in Tokyo. “(China) is also sending a signal to Tokyo that if it continues its current position vis-a-vis Taiwan that Beijing will continue these activities.”
China is using the deployments, including live-fire drills, uncrewed drone missions and voyages by entire aircraft carrier groups, to exert an unrelenting, long-term pressure on Japan without violating international maritime laws, analysts said.
“By repeatedly transiting waters around the (southwestern) Islands, China is gradually normalizing PLA Navy activity within the first island chain, expanding its operational experience and creating a pattern of accepted presence,” said Katsuya Yamamoto, director of the Tokyo-based Sasakawa Peace Foundation’s strategy and deterrence program.
The first island chain includes Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines.
“In other words, it is establishing facts on the ground, or rather at sea, that broaden its future freedom of action,” Yamamoto said.
In the seven weeks after Takaichi’s comment, the U.S. think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies logged a spike in “notable” PLA escalatory moves. Over 2025 overall, it said, China showed just a “slight increase” in the number of PLA naval vessels reported operating in waters around Japan, including an increase in the number of Chinese ships within the contiguous zone of the disputed Senkaku Islands, which China calls the Diaoyu.
Deployments near the uninhabited, Japanese-controlled Senkakus have “remained at very high levels” over the past year as before, while joint Sino-Russian missions around Japan and Chinese naval activity near the outlying Japanese islets around the Miyako Island “seem to have increased”, said Jeffrey Kingston, a professor specializing in Asian studies and history at Temple University, Japan Campus.
Chinese and Russian aircraft patrolled in June over the Sea of Japan, followed by a joint naval passage in July in the Miyako Strait near outlying Japanese islets. Chinese and Russian surveillance aircraft did five separate flights near Japan in October.
Spokespeople for the Chinese ministries of foreign affairs and national defense have called China’s military actions fair, valid and peaceful.
China is probably using military moves as one in a series of measures – some economic – to get back at Takaichi for her November 2025 remarks, Kingston said. “They haven’t forgotten, that’s for sure,” he said. “They are in various ways trying to put the screws on her.”
Officials in Beijing still want a retraction of the prime minister’s November 2025 comments but it’s unlikely, Kingston believes.
The Japanese government has verbally protested against Chinese military moves, tracked Chinese ships with its own, and scrambled fighter jets.
Tokyo is now considering a 70 trillion to 80 trillion yen (as high as $508 billion) defense spending plan for the five-year period beginning in April 2027, up from 43 trillion yen in the previous half-decade span, Japanese media outlets have reported.
“As the security environment becomes increasingly severe, cooperation with the ally and like-minded countries is indispensable to peace and stability in the region,” Japan’s Ministry of Defense said in an Oct. 29 statement after a meeting with defense officials from Australia, the Philippines and the United States.
The ministry, it said, “will continue to take advantage of various opportunities to further strengthen such cooperation.”

articles.title: US and Russia to oppose talks on limiting autonomous weapons
articles.snippet: Major arms producers the U.S. and Russia look set to oppose a push at a global meeting to launch negotiations on legally binding rules for autonomous weapons.
articles.full_text:
Major arms producers the United States and Russia look set to oppose a push at a global meeting in Geneva this week to launch negotiations on legally binding rules for autonomous weapons, diplomats and rights groups said.
The rise of artificial intelligence has boosted development of drones, robots, tanks, submarines and other military hardware capable of killing without human involvement. Semi-autonomous, AI-assisted weapons have already been used in Ukraine, Sudan and the Middle East, despite ethical concerns.
The UN-hosted meeting from Monday is due to decide whether to start talks for a legally binding pact on prohibitions and regulations for Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS).
But while most of the 128 states party to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons support that, major military nations including the U.S., Russia and Israel oppose it, arguing that existing humanitarian law is sufficient.
In a video message, the UN secretary-general urged states to agree to move towards negotiating a legally binding instrument including clear prohibitions and restrictions.
“The nature of warfare is changing. New technologies — including autonomous weapon systems — present new humanitarian, legal, ethical and security challenges,” Antonio Guterres said.
But Russia stymied the start of talks on Monday with its objection to a procedural rule allowing observers, including the EU and non-governmental organisations, to take the floor. Delegates including Ireland and Canada opposed that.
The International Committee of the Red Cross, along with the pope, has also warned of the dangers from autonomous weapons.
‘Dystopian reality’
“Machines should never be allowed to decide who lives and dies on a battlefield but that is the dystopian reality that is fast approaching,” said Verity Coyle from Human Rights Watch, which is also urging the Review Conference to take firm action.
Two diplomats told Reuters the discussions would be challenging but that a compromise may be found by the end of the week. All options are on the table, from legally binding to non-legally binding, as well as a hybrid agreement with both elements, one of the diplomats said.
Campaigners say autonomous weapons systems can behave unpredictably, raising the risk of fatal errors.
Anna Hehir, head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute – a US-based nonprofit organization focused on reducing the risks of advanced technologies, including AI — said LAWS were no longer science fiction, pointing to media reporting of early use of fully autonomous systems in Ukraine.
The U.S. favors guidelines over binding rules on LAWS, arguing that international law already provides a framework to govern warfare. It has proposed a five-year mandate for talks towards a non-binding agreement.
Hehir told Reuters the U.S. and Russia would probably seek to water down any outcome as they did in September with a text about autonomous weapons and their potential for harm.
The chair of this week’s talks has proposed a two-year mandate to negotiate a legally binding protocol.
The UK, Germany and France propose negotiations on an instrument that leaves open whether it would be legally binding or not, Coyle told Reuters.

articles.title: Italy backs rapid German membership path into GCAP fighter program
articles.snippet: Italy has strongly denied a press report suggesting it opposes granting Germany partner status on the GCAP fighter program, claiming instead it fully backs German membership.
articles.full_text:
ROME — Italy has strongly denied a press report suggesting it opposes granting Germany partner status on the GCAP fighter program, claiming instead it fully backs German membership.
The unusually long rebuttal from the Italian ministry of defense followed a report in the Financial Times on Saturday that defense minister Guido Crosetto used a video conference call last week with other representatives of the Italian-UK-Japan fighter to oppose making Germany a member.
Berlin is mulling signing up to the program after the collapse of its talks with France to develop a rival sixth-generation jet.
The press report suggested Italy was pushing to hand Germany observer status on the program rather than full membership, although it did quote an Italian official saying German membership could follow.
Within hours of the report appearing, Crosetto’s ministry fired off a statement calling the article “entirely misleading”, adding it “does not reflect the position Italy has consistently maintained.”
The statement agreed that it wanted Germany to obtain observer status, but in order to accelerate full membership status, not to delay or block it.
“Italy has always expressed its full willingness to welcome Germany into the program. Indeed, precisely to facilitate and accelerate this process, Italy proposed that Germany joins as an observer, as an immediate, Program information-sharing enabler towards subsequent full membership,” it added.
The statement added, “This proposal was not intended to limit Germany’s future role in the program. Quite the opposite: it was designed to speed up the conditions for its involvement as quickly as possible, while safeguarding the program’s progress and established timetable.”
The talks come as the GCAP program picks up speed after the three nation partners handed a £4.6 billion ($6.1 billion) development contract to their national champions building the jet in July.
Rome has spent €875 million ($970 million) this year on development.
Canada has meanwhile already taken observer status on the program.
The Italian statement said, “It is therefore totally false any reporting on opposition to Germany’s participation. Italy has demonstrated, through its actions and proposals, that it considers Germany’s involvement a positive opportunity.”
It added, “Our priority remains ensuring that GCAP proceeds according to its agreed schedule, while creating the conditions for new partners to join through a clear and effective process. Italy is supporting, without delay, all the conditions to welcome Germany’s participation in the GCAP as soon as possible.”

articles.title: Marine Corps doubles, extends contract for M27 rifles
articles.snippet: The service began replacing its infantry’s squad weapons with the M27 IAR in 2028 and will continue through 2028.
articles.full_text:
The Marine Corps more than doubled the contract ceiling with gunmaker Heckler & Koch for the M27 Infantry Automatic Rifle, or IAR.
According to the Nov. 6 notice, the contract value increased by $45.4 million, a jump from $39.23 million to $84.6 million. That price covers new guns, parts and associated equipment.
The notice came roughly eight months after the service revealed that it opted to keep the M27 rather than adopting the Army’s higher-caliber M7 rifle. In February, a Marine Corps spokesperson explained to Military Times that the M27 was better suited “for our close combat formations” and aligned with its service requirements.
Although the Marine Corps has tested and fielded the M27 for more than 15 years, the service expanded use of the weapon system in 2018 with a five-year contract for indefinite delivery/indefinite quantity, or IDIQ.
Although the M27 is the Marine Corps’ current service weapon for all infantry battalions, it was originally only meant to replace the M249 Squad Automatic Weapon, or SAW. However, because of its size, capabilities, and reliability, the service made it standard issue for the infantry, replacing the legacy M4A1 and M16A4 systems.
In 2018, Marine Corps spokesmen explained said the M27 provides “the necessary increase in lethality” as the weapon system “has proven to be the best overall fighting rifle” and they predicted “an immediate increase in overall combat capability.”
Like its predecessors, the M27 is chambered for 5.56mm NATO rounds and is can use the same 30-round magazine. Modeled after the HK416 — the weapon used to kill Osama bin Laden — the M27 uses a short-stroke gas-piston operating system, but it features a barrel at 16.5 inches. The longer barrel gives the M27 greater range.
Since fielding the M27, the service has also adopted new standard equipment like suppressors and lasers as well as capabilities for the platform. Earlier this year, Marines began new service-level training to shoot down small unmanned aerial systems, or sUASs (aka drones), with the M27 and other small arms.
According to the notice, Heckler & Koch will continue to supply the service with the M27 through April 2028. Most of the manufacturing will occur at the gunmaker’s facility in Oberndorf, Germany, and the rest in Columbus, Georgia.

articles.title: Vulcan failure deepens concerns over US military launch capacity
articles.snippet: The failed launch could further delay the rocket’s return to national security missions as the Space Force works to expand its launch options.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Sunday’s failed launch of United Launch Alliance’s (ULA) Vulcan rocket adds to growing concerns about the Space Force’s hopes to dramatically increase its launch cadence over the next few years.
The Vulcan suffered an anomaly about 10 minutes after liftoff, preventing the rocket from reaching orbit and destroying 40 satellites for Amazon LEO’s planned broadband network for low-Earth orbit. The failure will likely trigger a lengthy investigation that could ground the rocket for months, further limiting the number of US rockets available for both national security and commercial customers.
The incident further cements SpaceX’s near monopoly on US space launch. Aside from Vulcan, SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy are the only rockets currently authorized to carry critical payloads under the Space Force’s National Security Space Launch (NSSL) Phase 3 Lane 2 program — given that Blue Origin’s New Glenn also remains grounded following a launch pad explosion in May.
“We can hope that whatever caused this problem gets fixed. We can hope that Vulcan, New Glenn and other medium-lift vehicles come online soon, but this is really the same place we have been for the last several years,” Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Breaking Defense. “But the launch bottleneck is real and set to get worse.”
While the failed Vulcan mission was carrying a commercial payload, it was also designed to serve as an important step toward the rocket’s return to the Space Force’s NSSL program.
Vulcan was grounded by the service in late February due to persistent problems with its solid rocket boosters. By Oct. 1, the Space Force reassigned six NSSL missions previously manifested on Vulcan to SpaceX.
ULA has yet to publicly announce the cause of the rocket’s failure shortly after liftoff, but the problem appears to have occurred in the booster stage, according to a report in Ars Technica. If the rocket’s BE-4 engines were involved, the failure could also have implications for Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which uses the same engines.
“If the issue is with the BE-4 that is a particularly thorny problem — for the Pentagon, for NASA, for Amazon and for anyone who needs a ride to space,” Swope said.
Meanwhile, SpaceX is making progress with development of its new, fully reusable Starship super-heavy launch vehicle. During a test flight on Nov. 14, the company demonstrated for the first time its ability to capture the rocket’s massive upper stage.
The company plans to shift all of its own launch operations to Starship around 2030, phasing out its Falcon rockets In September, SpaceX stopped taking commercial orders for Falcon rides post 2028. The company has also yet to announce plans to offer Starship launches to commercial or military customers.
Those decisions have caused widespread concerns about a potential multiyear gap between demand for US launch services and available capacity.
“I don’t see a magic wand here. I mean, the only thing that could happen is that somebody persuades Elon to keep Falcon 9 flying until there are viable alternatives,” said Martin Halliwell, of Luxembourg-based private equity firm New Space Capital.
