articles.title: As exquisite radars become targets, smaller tactical sensors take on a bigger role
articles.snippet: [Sponsored] Record demand for radars is accelerating investment in manufacturing capacity and a distributed supply chain.
articles.full_text:
Missile and drone attacks in Ukraine and the Middle East are putting new pressure on the radars that underpin air-and-missile defense, driving demand for systems that can be fielded faster, in greater numbers, and be networked across a wider area.
Breaking Defense spoke with Joe Mollo, senior director of Advanced Programs at Leonardo DRS RADA Technologies business unit (DRS RADA), about surging demand for tactical radars, the push to expand manufacturing capacity, and how a new generation of sensors could change the way air defenses are built.
Breaking Defense: There’s been a lot of attention in Washington on defense-industrial base capacity and resilience, particularly in response to the new threats we’re facing in the CENTCOM region. Summarize what you view as the rapidly evolving threat?
Mollo: The Iranian-designed Shahed/Geran loitering munition has become the poster-child of this new threat environment, and it’s evolving on multiple axes at once. In Ukraine, we’ve seen single-day tactical drone employment exceed 10,000 units along the front line, while the long-range strike variant aimed at cities has simultaneously gone jet-powered – now representing over half of deep-strike sorties, shortening the already challenging warning time of the original propeller-driven design, requiring a defense that detects sooner, engages further, and acts faster.
Against Israel, we’ve now seen three massive, coordinated Iranian state barrages – April 2024, October 2024, and the 12-day war in June 2025 – each launching hundreds to over a thousand ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones directly from Iranian soil. Layer on top of that the grinding, continuous fire from Iran’s proxies: 15,000-20,000-plus rockets, missiles, and drones from Hezbollah and the Houthis. The threat is constant and pervasive, requiring a defense that scales, costs less, and is mobile.
Operation Epic Fury and the parallel Houthi Red Sea campaign showed this threat has outgrown any single theater. Iran demonstrated both the willingness and the reach to strike across the entire Gulf – and, more troubling for us, the ability to take out major US IAMD sensor infrastructure.
Ballistic missiles and low-cost one-way attack drones together damaged or destroyed radar systems in Qatar, Jordan, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, and Kuwait – including a $1.1 billion early-warning radar. Those systems will take years to replace.
This requires a defense that can be produced faster and has a cost that supports dispersed operations for survivability. Such systems need to look at things that are low and slow or low and fast, the cruise missiles, the Group 3 drones. Tactical radars for survivability’s sake and the ability to look low have become a real hot item. If you’re going to have a big radar protecting a geographic area and that’s the first thing that gets hit, well now I need smaller, more dispersed radar capabilities.
The real issue is whether the US industrial base produces sensor and interceptor systems at the quantity and speed that this evolving threat demands in order to protect US and allied interests.
How does this translate to DRS RADA?
As a leading global supplier of tactical radar systems for counter-UAS, air-defense, and missile-defense applications, DRS RADA is feeling the stress of significant demand across both US and international markets. In the United States, demand is increasing from the Department of War and the Department of Homeland Security, as well as through Foreign Military Sales (FMS) and Direct Commercial Sales (DCS) to international partners.
DRS RADA also continues to see sustained demand from customers in the Middle East and Eastern Europe served through its non-US operations. This is reflected in record bookings in each of the past two quarters, underscoring both the breadth and urgency of this demand.
Ukraine came in at the end of 2023 with a single order in which they ordered more than we had sold the prior two years. All of a sudden we’re getting this tremendous demand for tactical radars.
Additionally, there is an increased emphasis on robust homeland missile defense, especially in light of the operational lessons demonstrating the vulnerability of our current inventory of long-range sensors. Looking at the Golden Dome concept, these expensive radars, which are necessary for your long-range ballistic missiles, are the first to be hit. And, oh by the way, they take four or five years to produce and cost half a billion to a billion dollars.
In response, we looked at any way we can use smaller tactical radars in a disaggregated way. This would include geographically dispersed sensors that are more affordable and manufacturable at scale, that can be networked to provide the coverage, resilience, and mission performance traditionally associated with a few exquisite systems. DRS RADA’s tactical radar portfolio is well aligned with this shift toward disaggregated, networked sensing.
DRS RADA also supports numerous prime contractors and system integrators that are responding to the same market demand. These customers require close engineering and program support to integrate DRS RADA radar systems into complete mission solutions spanning the detect-to-effect chain. As a result, growth in radar-unit demand is accompanied by increased requirements for product development, systems integration, technical support, and manufacturing resources.
Together, these dynamics – higher demand volumes, shorter delivery timelines, and increasingly challenging customer requirements – are driving substantial investment in accelerated product development and expanded manufacturing and test capacity.
How is DRS RADA addressing the surge in demand?
The 2022 merger with Leonardo DRS has been instrumental in enabling the company to scale in response to growing customer demand. This merger has enabled us to increase R&D investment to accelerate new-product development, capitalize expanded manufacturing and test capacity, and add the technical and business infrastructure needed to build and sustain a global presence.
DRS RADA currently manufactures six radar models spanning a range of sizes, power levels, and missions. We continue to sustain and advance these models through ongoing improvements informed by requirements derived from extensive operational deployments. For example, these changes may support new technical requirements, such as new electronic counter-countermeasures, ECCM, threats and integration requirements.
DRS RADA is releasing two new radar models this month, the result of significant R&D investment and extensive development, integration, and testing over the past several years.
In terms of capital investment, the company has committed to expanding capacity in the communities that have supported our growth, while leveraging its broader international footprint to strengthen the supply chain for critical materials. At our Germantown, Maryland, facility, RADA has expanded its engineering and manufacturing workforce from 30 to 150 employees with 60 more planned for early 2027.
Our footprint has increased nearly 10-fold and our complex test facilities by four times. We are planning another wave of expansion to accommodate our newest product, the cxMHR (RPS-502), which is larger and more complex than any of our other systems, requiring its own dedicated production and test facilitation. And we’ve got another expansion following what we’re doing right now.
We’ve been in Montgomery County for the entire time we’ve been in the US and we wanted to stay there, stay there with the people that have worked with us all that time, stay with the community that supported us. So we’ve made all that investment right at home in Germantown, Maryland.
However, our global development and manufacturing footprint has undertaken expansion across our multiple facilities similar in scale to our US operations. These facilities are located in operational areas of conflict or where regional restrictions require a physical presence. One of the benefits of this distributed manufacturing footprint is that it improves DRS RADA’s supply-chain resilience and cost efficiency by enabling each location to source appropriate materials from its respective regional market, which can then be made available company wide, reducing dependence on any single supplier base or geography.
What does the cxMHR bring operationally?
As I noted earlier, the cxMHR is significantly larger, more powerful, and more complex than our other radar models and represents a major technology step forward that delivers a clear operational advantage in the medium-range tactical radar market.
The cxMHR operates in C-band, which occupies a very useful middle ground. It provides the high-resolution and precision-tracking performance typically associated with higher-frequency X-band systems while offering range and weather benefits similar to S-band.
What is particularly unique and important is that the cxMHR uses a fully digital aperture. Like all of our radars, the cxMHR is a software-defined active electronically scanned array (AESA) system. AESA is the current state of the art for tactical radars, giving users tremendous flexibility to tailor performance for a specific mission or to support multiple missions simultaneously, all through software control. This is particularly important for evolving missions or multi-mission requirements and for resilience against electronic attack.
AESA technology represents a meaningful distinction from both conventional phased-array and metamaterial-based approaches. A conventional passive phased-array radar relies on a centralized transmitter and phase control across the aperture, which provides electronic beam steering, but less independent control over the individual radiating elements and less flexibility to generate or manage multiple, mission-specific functions simultaneously. Metamaterial apertures performance is far less effective in mitigating electronic attack because it is closely linked to the electromagnetic response of the physical surface and requires iterative aperture-specific optimization to achieve a particular use case.
With a fully digital array, the cxMHR takes AESA another step forward. The cxMHR’s fully digital AESA architecture provides true, independent, per-element control across the transmit/receive aperture. This gives the radar exceptional ability to tailor beams, waveforms, power distribution, and radar-resource allocation rapidly and repeatedly via digital control.
The operational advantages are profound. These include: up to 40 times faster volume scan; precision beam pointing, a narrower main beam, less SNR loss, longer detection range, and less multi-path interference; simultaneous search, track, and jammer localization beams; ECCM and EMI performance with less clutter and better jamming suppression; independent element calibration and control for less loss and graceful degradation; and frequency diversity for reduced multipath elevation errors and reduced RCS fluctuation, resulting in a higher Pd.
If it gets shot, you’re not going to take out half of the radar. You’re going to take out maybe one of these elements, maybe four of them. The radar will still continue to work. It’s not a spinner. It gives you the whole 360-degree constant view, and there’s no moving parts in the antenna assembly.
In terms of dealing with jammers and interference from other sources, there’s less clutter and more resistance to jamming.
With true per-element digital control, the cxMHR can make mission-driven adjustments through digital control in a faster, more repeatable, and more deterministic manner.
What are your thoughts on the future of DRS RADA?
DRS RADA is well positioned to help the United States and its allies address the rapidly evolving threats we’re seeing in the CENTCOM region and future battlespaces. Since entering the tactical radar market eight years ago, DRS RADA has consistently invested in technology, product performance, and responsiveness to operational user requirements.
From its first prototype, DRS RADA has designed its radars around gallium nitride (GaN) technology and software-defined AESA architectures. GaN enables higher performance in a smaller, lighter, and more power-efficient package than legacy gallium arsenide based (GaAs) systems. While the US continues to pay for vendors to upgrade its tactical-radar inventory from GaAs to GaN, DRS RADA’s radar portfolio was designed around GaN from the outset.
Equally important, DRS RADA’s products have been shaped by extensive operational experience and direct user feedback. It wouldn’t be out of the realm of possibility to say that more of our radars have been shot than some of our competitors have ever produced. We continue to sustain and advance our radar models through extensive R&D investment, incorporating improvements that address evolving mission requirements and emerging threats.
DRS RADA has always operated under a startup mentality with continuous innovation. It’s served us really well and it continues to serve us really well because our adversaries have that same pace of change.
DRS RADA radars led the way for US capabilities in mobile short-range air defense, counter-UAS, and active protection system missions. Building on that foundation, the company continues to deliver high-performing tactical radars and develop integrated sensor solutions that help warfighters detect, track, and respond to the new and evolving threats they face in battle.
That last quarter that just ended was a record breaker like none we’ve ever seen. The quarter before that was a record breaker like none that we’ve ever seen. It just doesn’t stop; the demand just keeps coming.

articles.title: Army’s G-TEAD expands OTA awards to push more vendors to prototyping stage
articles.snippet: The Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate is now awarding up to six Other Transaction Authorities as opposed to just one following its Accelerated Capability Events.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Army directorate tasked with getting tech into the hands of soldiers within 180 days or less is increasing its use of Other Transaction Authority (OTA) contracts in order to help additional vendors reach the prototyping stage, according to senior service leaders.
Previously, the Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate (G-TEAD), under the Army’s Pathway for Innovation and Technology (PIT), awarded one OTA to a vendor after its Accelerated Capability Events, or ACEs, where vendors would show off tech with a technology readiness level of six or above. Now, the Army will be awarding five to six OTAs, as part of a conscious effort to expand the industrial base.
“The awarding of the six contracts is our way of allowing these small and medium-sized businesses to understand that when you participate in an ACE, if you make it through the competition, what’s waiting for you on the back end of that potentially is an OTA,” Col. Christopher Hill, director of the G-TEAD told reporters Friday. “This is a change to bring more people under the umbrella contractually.”
The Army’s Service Component Commands provide the demand signal for what type of technology the G-TEAD seeks out. Once that demand signal is clear, the directorate posts white papers for that technology and selects about 15 vendors to participate in the ACEs, which then potentially leads to OTAs.
Though this change will bring more OTAs, this doesn’t necessarily mean more vendors will receive production contracts. When the G-TEAD previously awarded just one OTA, it was a prototyping OTA. Now, the up to six OTAs provide funds for vendors to participate in a 45-day long operational assessments where they get more soldier and senior leader feedback, resulting in up to one to three OTAs for vendors to develop a prototype, Hill explained.
The operational assessments add an “operational flavor” and test new capabilities in an “actual mission” environment, Hill said. He added that it is “100 percent our expectation that the next time we see these systems, they are better than what we just saw during [the ACE] demonstration.”
The change to award more OTAs began with the ACE that recently concluded in Hawaii. The exercise was conducted in coordination with the Army’s Pacific Command to find autonomous ground vehicles and coinciding command and control systems capable of sustainment and casualty evacuation missions in logistically challenging environments, Hill said. The G-TEAD selected its winners, but has not yet disclosed the vendors.
Further, Hill said awarding more OTAs incentivizes vendors to come out to such events, since companies often incur hefty costs for packing up and moving all their equipment. It also allows them the bragging rights of having won an OTA, even if it’s not for a prototype award, which could make them more desirable in future competitions, Hill said.
For the ACE that just wrapped up in Hawaii, some companies that were awarded the initial OTAs, but not prototype OTAs, could have better success in other regions, Col. Shermoan Daiyaan, director of the PIT, said.
“Some capabilities may not be as useful in the Pacific — in the jungle — as it may be more applicable in the ACE that’s happening in Europe right now,” he said. “So it doesn’t throw them out. It just says that for this particular ACE, they didn’t perform as well […] so we may invite them out to a future ACE.”

articles.title: Navy eyes ‘operational employment’ of key UUV programs, admiral says
articles.snippet: The Navy is expected to receive its third Orca prototype vessel “soon,” according to a service official.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Navy is getting closer to operationally using several unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs) — specifically the Orca, with the service set to receive its third “soon,” according to the commander of Submarine Forces for the US Pacific Fleet.
Additionally, the Navy is making progress on the Combat Autonomous Maritime Platform (CAMP) XLUUV, which is the Navy and the Department of Innovation Unit’s initiative to quickly prototype and field XLUUVs, as well as the Dragonfish large displacement UUV (LDUUV), which replaced the Navy’s nixed Snakehead LDUUV program.
“Those are all progressing toward meaningful operational employment,” Rear Adm. Chris Cavanaugh said Thursday. “Those systems complement our crewed platforms, expand our reach, increase our operational flexibility, and allow us to accept risks that we wouldn’t take with manned submarines.”
The Orca program is the Navy’s first XLUUV initiative, launched in 2017, and aimed at laying undersea mines. The first test vehicle was delivered in 2023 and the first prototype vehicle was delivered in 2025, according to the Government Accountability Office. The vessel has a range of up to 6,500 nautical miles to support “monthslong, long-range missions” and can accommodate a host of mission payloads, according to Boeing, which makes the vehicle.
Capt. Michael Linn, the program manager for the Undersea Warfare Program Management Office, said that the service is nearing the end of production plans for Orca, and that two of the three prototype vessels have already been delivered. Ultimately, the program will lay the groundwork for other UUV programs like CAMP, he said.
“We’re going to get our third one delivered soon, and that is going to wrap up a long and arduous process of getting Orca over the finish line,” Linn said on Friday. “Once we get it in our hands, we’re going to continue to characterize it. We’re going to put it through its paces and figure out what it really does well and what it doesn’t do well. But the point is I’m fully intent on getting it employed and characterized. CAMP, we’re going to build on what we learned from Orca.”

articles.title: Match fined $10 million for alleged Tinder privacy violations
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Ireland’s data protection regulator will fine the Match Group as a result of the dating app Tinder allegedly failing to provide users with their personal data held by the company upon request.
articles.full_text:
Match fined $10 million for alleged Tinder privacy violations
Ireland’s data protection regulator will fine the Match Group €11 million ($10 million) as a result of the dating app Tinder allegedly failing to provide users with their personal data held by the company upon request.
The country’s Data Protection Commission (DPC) alleged Tinder offers a self-service tool known as Download My Data that purports to let users access a complete copy of their information, but in reality fails to provide all of it.
Some categories of data were left out without users’ knowledge or were only supplied as summaries, the regulator’s press release said. The agency also alleges data provided by the tool did not comply with Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation’s right of access standard, which requires controllers to let consumers know if their personal information is being processed.
“These tools do not need to provide a complete copy of personal data, but they must be fair and transparent to individuals regarding the extent of the data provided,” DPC deputy commissioner Graham Doyle said in a statement. The probe was launched in January 2020.
Tens of thousands of users accessed the tool during the nearly six-year-long inquiry, according to the press release.
The DPC issued an order requiring Match to begin complying with the data processing rule within three months. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: Italian regulator fines Meta $886 million for violating data privacy law
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The crackdown on Meta’s Facebook platform involved the company’s alleged use of its “camera roll” suggestions option, launched in 2023, to browse Android users’ photo galleries to recommend posts they could enhance with personal photos and videos.
articles.full_text:
Italian regulator fines Meta $886 million for violating data privacy law
Italy’s data protection regulator announced a €805 million ($886 million) fine against Meta on Saturday, saying the social media giant accessed user photos and videos without their specific consent or properly informing them.
The fine, announced Saturday, is one of the biggest the Italian regulator — known as the Garante — has ever issued.
The crackdown on Meta’s Facebook platform involved the company’s alleged use of its “camera roll” suggestions option, launched in 2023, to browse Android users’ photo galleries to recommend posts they could enhance with personal photos and videos. In addition to the photos and videos, the regulator said, Facebook accessed related metadata.
The investigation found Meta asked users to access their camera roll through a single permission that “applies across the entire app covering multiple features with different requirements,” according to a Garante press release.
The permission is preceded by a “non-specific notice” to enable other features, the press release said, failing to make clear to users that they are consenting to suggestions from the camera roll, the regulator said. It also alleged the feature was turned on by default.
“When given in full, such permission allows the app to access the entire photo library on the device, usually on a permanent basis, without the user or [regulators] being able to verify what information is actually being used,” the press release said.
The practice violates Italian data protection regulations safeguarding “the smartphone as part of the individual’s private sphere,” according to a Garate press release.
“Consequently, any access to the information stored on such devices requires free and informed consent, regardless of whether data is transmitted or any harm occurs,” the press release said.
Meta had argued the Garante lacked jurisdiction to issue the fine, but the regulator dismissed that claim.
A Meta spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but told other news outlets in a statement that the company strongly disagrees with the decision and plans to appeal what it called the “disproportionate” fine amount.
The tech giant has been under fire worldwide in recent months, losing multiple court cases in the U.S., including an October decision in which the company was fined $25 billion for deceiving consumers about how it uses their data.
In addition to the fine, the Garante has ordered Meta to make several changes in the next 60 days, including by obtaining consent through a request that is “separate and specific to the feature” and clearly explaining what it is used for. Meta also must begin disabling the option by default.
The unusually high fine is due to the fact that about 20 million Italian Android users were impacted, the long time period over which the violation occurred and the company’s lack of cooperation during the probe, the press release said.
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: King Charles opens new HQ for National Cyber Force, UK’s offensive hacking unit
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: A building near the Lancashire village of Samlesbury in northwest England is officially the headquarters for the secretive unit that runs the Britain's offensive cyber operations.
articles.full_text:
King Charles opens new HQ for National Cyber Force, UK’s offensive hacking unit
King Charles III on Monday opened the new headquarters of Britain’s National Cyber Force, the secretive unit that runs the country’s offensive cyber operations against hostile states, terrorists and criminals.
Staff are already working in the building near the Lancashire village of Samlesbury in northwest England, named Ribble House after the nearby river and Ribble Valley. The government chose the village as the force’s permanent home five years ago and committed £5 billion ($6.5 billion) to the NCF through 2030.
The NCF brings together staff from the cyber and signals intelligence agency GCHQ, the Ministry of Defence, the Secret Intelligence Service (MI6) and the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory. Officials say it carries out operations every day.
“In an age of radical uncertainty, contested geopolitics, and rapidly changing technology, the NCF keeps the country safe by delivering high-impact cyber operations every single day against those who threaten our interests,” said GCHQ Director Anne Keast-Butler who showed the king around the site.
As first reported by Recorded Future News, a new commander is currently in charge at the NCF, replacing Air Vice-Marshal Tim Neal-Hopes in September, although officials have yet to name them publicly. Neal-Hopes took over in October 2023 from James Babbage, a former GCHQ officer who subsequently moved to the National Crime Agency.
To date, the NCF has rarely discussed its work in public, saying disclosures would undermine the effects of its covert operations. In a 2023 doctrine paper, it described its operations as “accountable, precise, and calibrated,” in a way that was fundamentally different from those practiced by Britain’s adversaries.
Gen. Sir Rob Magowan, commander of Cyber and Specialist Operations Command, said: “The opening of the National Cyber Force’s new headquarters marks a significant milestone in strengthening the UK’s ability to combat threats in an increasingly contested world.
“We must be ready to confront, deter and prevail in the cyber domain, taking the initiative against those who threaten our national security. The National Cyber Force plays a vital role in giving the UK that advantage,” he added.
British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called the headquarters “a major investment in the North West, in defence innovation, and in keeping our country safe.”
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: “As hostile actors use cyberattacks to disrupt our way of life and cause us harm, our world class intelligence agencies ensure that we can tackle those threats head-on.”
Ribble House’s ceremonial opening comes on the same day a House of Lords committee warned the country is “underprepared” for “potentially catastrophic risks” including cyberattacks from Russia, China and Iran.
The committee said the government “appears complacent” and stressed the “need to move fast to turn things around.”
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: Russia denies intercepting Romanian government emails
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Russia has denied accusations that its state-backed hackers targeted a Romanian government institution in an attempt to intercept emails exchanged with NATO and the European Union.
articles.full_text:
Russia denies intercepting Romanian government emails
Russia has denied accusations that its state-backed hackers targeted a Romanian government institution in an attempt to intercept emails exchanged with NATO and the European Union.
The Russian Embassy in Bucharest on Monday dismissed the allegations as fabricated, accusing Romanian intelligence services of spreading false claims about Moscow's involvement in cyberattacks.
"This is yet another fabrication by the Romanian intelligence services, part of their ongoing narrative about Russia's mythical 'hybrid attacks,'" the embassy said in a statement published on Telegram in response to questions from Reuters.
The embassy accused Romanian authorities of trying to discredit Russia and said Bucharest had provided no concrete evidence to support its claims.
The denial comes days after Romania's domestic intelligence agency (SRI) said it had detected and stopped a cyberattack attributed to Turla, a long-running Russian espionage group linked to Moscow's Federal Security Service (FSB).
According to the agency, the hackers infiltrated the systems of an unidentified government institution in December 2025 by exploiting vulnerabilities in Microsoft software.
Romanian cybersecurity specialists contained the intrusion and restored the affected email service, the agency said, adding that investigators had found no evidence that sensitive information had been stolen.
The disclosure followed research published earlier this month by Slovak cybersecurity firm ESET, which uncovered a previously unknown hacking toolkit used by Turla to compromise government email servers in Romania and Kazakhstan.
According to ESET, the malware deployed against the Romanian target was specifically configured to collect emails exchanged with NATO and EU institutions.
Romania's intelligence agency said it was also investigating other potentially related cyber operations linked to Russia.
Moscow has for years denied accusations of carrying out cyberattacks and other hostile operations against Western countries.

is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. UK leaves client-side scanning out of new child safety rules
Britain’s online safety regulator Ofcom said Monday it does not have the power to make technology companies scan people’s personal devices for child abuse images, a major statement amid the ongoing controversy about abusers’ use of commodity encrypted messaging platforms.
Ofcom made the announcement while finalizing new rules under the Online Safety Act. The regulator said it “does not have powers under the Act to regulate devices” in response to campaigners calling for the scanning technology while expressing concern child abusers were using encrypted services to escape detection.
Under the finalized rules, large technology platforms will have to use tools to proactively detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM) — even when that material has never been seen before and has not been digitally fingerprinted— but only for content that users share publicly.
For encrypted chats, Ofcom’s revised guidance allows the platforms to judge a whole group based on its profile picture, description, or coded terms backed by a British police report. The regulator acknowledged this kind of enforcement “may interfere significantly with users’ privacy.”
Under the rules set out Monday, which would take effect in February 2027 if approved by Parliament, all platforms that host user-shared content must permanently ban adults who are discovered to be sharing CSAM or to be grooming children.
There will be exceptions for bans, including for victims and potentially for those who promptly report unwanted images, designed to address the risk that CSAM could be shared to harass its recipients. Suspected terrorist, hate, suicide and self-harm content must also be kept out of children's recommendation feeds.
The regulator also said it would not for now be setting limits on how other platform users can comment, send gifts, or record children’s livestreams as the government’s proposed ban on under-16s using social media made those protections unnecessary.
Client-side scanning, a mechanism of running those tools on users’ own phones or computers before the messages are encrypted and sent, is a controversial topic.
Supporters argue it is the only way to find CSAM exchanged over end-to-end encrypted services, while security researchers and privacy campaigns argue scanning on device breaks the promise of encryption.
Apple explored the approach in 2021 when it announced a client-side scanning system that would check content on-device to see if it depicted child abuse. Following criticisms, Apple quietly shelved the plan in 2022.
Ofcom did not rule out any introduction of client-side scanning in the future, but instead left the issue to a different part of the Online Safety Act. Section 121 of the law allows the regulator to issue a “technology notice” ordering a company to use accredited software to find CSAM, including in private messages.
Under the law, before Ofcom can issue such a notice the technology must be accredited against accuracy standards set by the government. Those standards only came into force in September, and Ofcom has not announced that any tool has yet been accredited.
The regulator said its rules would not apply in cases where they would “materially compromise the security” of a service, but it warned that mere high costs — or the need for design changes — would not be sufficient defenses on their own.
Ofcom also dropped plans, which had been proposed alongside the CSAM measures in June 2025, that would have required platforms to detect fraud automatically. It said it had “a high degree of confidence” only in detection tools for CSAM images, and that it would consult on how to tackle other harms next year.
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
articles.snippet: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world's most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
articles.full_text:
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).
Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.
The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.
The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.
Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].
Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.
The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.
IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.
Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.
The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.
Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.
Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.
A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.
That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.
More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.
Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.
Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

articles.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
articles.snippet: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month's Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws -- including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook -- and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.
November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.
This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.
According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.
Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.
Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.
“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”
Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.
Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.
Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).
“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”
Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.
Thank you as always. Your concern and actions for others is very much appreciated by all, including those not aware of it.

articles.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
articles.snippet: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
articles.full_text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.
The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.
Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.
“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.
“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”
All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.
As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

One useful technical distinction is that AS2650 is an autonomous system, not a single subnet. For an observed exit IP, investigators still need the timestamp, the then-current BGP origin and prefix, RDAP allocation data, and corroborating telemetry; registration or geolocation alone does not identify the device or the proxy customer. That matters when a residential proxy makes traffic look trusted simply because the address falls inside an organization’s announced space. articles.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
articles.snippet: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
articles.full_text:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”
The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.
Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).
The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.
Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.
Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.
Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.
In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.
Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.
That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.
Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linus Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].
The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”
Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”
“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”
Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.
“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”
The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.
“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”
